extracted.intended_audience: architects, art historians, students and practitioners of architectural ornament (especially Venetian/medieval)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for reading, judging, and designing Venetian medieval architectural ornament — focusing on material choice, color, sculpture, proportion, repetition, and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of color over sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the white capitals are sculptured below; only the white triangles are sculptured above. No colored triangle is touched with sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color as a primary visual element; leave colored stones largely unsculptured so their chromatic effect is preserved. Sculpture should be applied selectively to white (or neutral) elements so as not to destroy or compete with colored surfaces. Example: centre of group is color not sculpture to draw the eye to chequers of stone as much as to chiselling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal invasive finishing on colored stone
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch colored marbles with sculpture only as a 'mere sign of carefulness and finish, but at the same time destroying their colored surface as little as possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ornamenting colored stones, prefer very light incisions or etching rather than deep carving so the color/variegation remains intact. Examples: fine incisions of concentric hues or wreaths outlined on purple marble; the keystone worked with light incision to preserve surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrasting material to emphasize composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of black-and-white marble or dark touches to emphasize the centre of a chain, 'exactly as a painter would use a dark touch for a similar purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce darker or contrasting stones at focal points to create painterly emphasis and center the composition. Example: using black-and-white marble to mark the central triangle in the series to act as a visual anchor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied but ordered chequering and grouping of inlaid triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: The band is composed of triangles set close to each other in varied but not irregular relations; groups of seven triangles form repeatable units with specified arrangements for each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design inlaid patterns with deliberate order and variation: repeat group-types but vary their placement and the number of elements per side to respond to local dimensions. Avoid random irregularity; plan groups so that the overall series has internal symmetry and answer across the whole apse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and visibility tuned to viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament is thrown out in low and flat relief, intermediate spaces cut to depth (~1/4 inch), so the design is visible at the necessary distance (17 or 18 feet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose relief depth and clarity of motif with the intended viewing distance in mind. Simplicity of method and contrast (background fill or dark ground) improve legibility. Example: use low relief with a dark fill so trefoil motifs remain crisp at 17–18 feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful variation in repeated motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Trefoils are repeated five or six hundred times yet 'hardly ever twice of the same size'; the same leaf continually repeated but never identical in size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce systematic, purposeful variation in scale/shape of repeating motifs (as in nature) rather than mechanical uniformity. Measure and vary angles/widths deliberately (not by chance) to achieve a natural, lively effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match sculptural fineness to material quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Make chiselling finer where it is to go with variegated marbles, and use a bolder pattern with coarser brick and dark stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust level of detail to suit material: high-fidelity, delicate carving for precious/variegated marbles; bolder, simpler carving for rougher brick or darker stone, so sculpture harmonizes with material texture and color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use material and proportion to create hierarchical focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower (central) series is made more precious — no brick and three kinds of variegated marble — while the upper is subordinated by using brick and fewer marbles; proportions (height/acuity) are altered so one series is subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish visual priority by richer materials and denser ornament at focal zones, and make adjacent bands lighter or subtler by material choice and proportion changes (e.g., make upper triangles more acute/higher and lighter in effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate intentionality of structural adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: When structural or proportional differences occur (e.g., blanks at angles), draw the eye to them so they read as deliberate: increase height of upper triangles, add courses of plain bricks, or narrow bases to show design choice rather than accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an adjustment (to fit geometry or correct irregularity) might look like an error, emphasize it with a visible design decision so viewers perceive it as purposeful (e.g., change proportion, add a border course).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create rhythmic continuity across large structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance can be effected across the whole apse so that local imbalance (e.g., an inserted triangle without balance in its own group) is compensated on the other side of the apse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan ornament as part of a global system; accept local asymmetries if the total composition balances when read as a whole, even if not seen simultaneously from one viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit projection and inlay to mark architectural turns
rubrics_metrics.description: When the band turns an arch, reversed triangles of marble inlaid to equal depth but projecting beyond produce a sharp dark zigzag at their junctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes in depth/projection of inlaid elements to produce crisp lines at transitions (cornices, arches) and to articulate the turning of structural planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate use of rare/contrasting fragments to enhance pictorial effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A stone of awkward shape or rare color should be made conspicuous — e.g., using dark cold grey on one side and vigorous green on the other to contrast warm reds and purples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn irregularities or rare fragments into visual features by choosing contrasting colors to highlight them; this celebrates difficulty rather than concealing it and increases pictorial interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material selection according to function (strength vs decoration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yellow brick (strong, nearly vitrified) used for parts requiring strength; deep red porous brick used chiefly for decoration; marbles used for inlay and ornament in several kinds (white, veined, brecciated, green, purple, grey/black).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign materials by structural need and decorative intent: use durable, robust materials for load-bearing parts and more variegated/precious stones for decorative, focal components; exploit differing thicknesses and sizes for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful reuse of older fragments (spolia) with attention to key motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Fragments of older work are reused (turned inside out) but care is taken so that certain motifs (e.g., crosses) are left uninjured and centered in new pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When incorporating older carved elements, preserve salient iconographic features and integrate them so their important motifs remain legible and central rather than mutilated — both out of respect and to retain historical information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pavement and mosaic as coloristic foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pavement is composed of variegated marbles set with skillful arrangement of peacocks, lions, interlacing bands and chequers; Murano's pavement shows early Venetian spirit of color and dates (e.g., 1140).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat floors/mosaics as important color fields influencing the building's overall effect; use variegated fragments and strong patterning to contribute to the ensemble's chromatic richness and historical character.
